Use this page when a pregnancy or birth variable is your exposure, outcome or
covariate. It covers three groups of variables from the Medical Birth Register
(MFR): gestational age and size at birth, parity, and multiple births. For each
it says which column to use, where the register is weak, and what to write in
your methods.

The columns of each MFR table are in [Overview of
registers](register-reference.qmd#mfr---medical-birth-register), and this page
does not repeat them. The table below spells the names as DST (Statistics Denmark) does. The code
uses lower case, as after `rename_with(tolower)`. Check the names in your own
delivery with `colnames()`.

## Which table holds what {#tables}

The MFR has three eras with different tables, and the variable names differ
between them ([Bliddal et al.
2018](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10654-018-0356-1);
[Danish Health Data Authority (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen, SDS), register page](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/data-og-registre/nationale-sundhedsregistre/foedselsregisteret)).

| Variable                | 1997-2018 (`mfr`)                    | 2019 onwards (`mfr_nyfoedte`)       |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| Gestational age         | `gestationsalder_dage` (days)        | `Gestationsalder` (days), `GestationsalderUger` (full weeks) |
| Birth weight (g)        | `vaegt_barn`                         | `Vaegt_Barn`                        |
| Parity                  | `paritet`                            | `Paritet`                           |
| Multiple births         | `flerfoldsfoedsel_beregnet`, `barnsnummer_flerfoldsfoedsel` (child's number) | `AntalBoernIFoedslen` (children in the birth), `BarnsNummerIFoedslen` (child's number) |
| Birth serial number     | `foedselsloebenummer`                | `DW_EK_Foedsel` (birth event key)   |

Stillbirths from 1997 to 2018 are in a separate dataset, `mfrdfoed`, with
gestational age in `gestationsalder_uger` and
`gestationsalder_dage_efter_uger` (full weeks and the days after them), not in
total days ([SDS, documentation 1997-2018, tables
`Doedsfoedsler_blanket` and
`Hjemmefoedsler_blanket`](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/Media/638650989745673989/Dokumentation_Foedselsregisteret_1997_2018.xlsx)).
The 2019 table holds live births and stillbirths together.

Both gestational age columns are in **days**, so divide by 7 for weeks. SDS
gives the example 283 days for 40 weeks and 3 days ([SDS, documentation from
2019](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/Media/638650989728109987/Dokumentation_Foedselsregisteret_2019_og_frem.xlsx)).

Before 1997 DST has no MFR table, and its fertility datasets (`ftbarn`,
`ftforael`) do not hold gestational age. See [the pre-1997
period](register-reference.qmd#ftbarn).

**Two things change in 2019.**

- **The population.** Up to 2018 the register holds births in Denmark to
  mothers with a Danish CPR (the Civil Registration System) number. From 2019 it holds births in Denmark
  whether or not the mother has one, so a study that crosses 2019 compares two
  populations ([Family links](family-links.qmd#mfr)).
- **Missing values.** In the 2019 table numeric fields such as `Vaegt_Barn`
  and `Paritet` use -1 for "not stated", not `NA`. Recode -1 to `NA` before you
  compute anything, or a mean is pulled down ([the Nyfoedte
  section](register-reference.qmd#mfr-nyfoedte) lists the fields).

## Gestational age and preterm birth {#gestational-age}

### Missing values and cleaning {#ga-quality}

Gestational age is missing for 8% of births in 1997 and 1% from 2001. SDS does
not clean the register after entry, so unrealistic gestational ages and birth
weights stay in the data ([Bliddal et al.
2018](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10654-018-0356-1)). Look at the distribution
before you categorise, and decide on a rule for implausible values that you
can describe in the methods.

### Preterm categories {#preterm}

WHO (World Health Organization) defines preterm birth as a birth before 37 completed weeks and divides it
into three groups ([WHO fact sheet on preterm
birth](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/preterm-birth)).

| Group                 | Completed weeks |
| --------------------- | --------------- |
| Extremely preterm     | Below 28        |
| Very preterm          | 28 to below 32  |
| Moderate to late preterm | 32 to below 37 |

Report the groups, not only the composite, when your question is about causes
or outcomes that differ along the range. In days the cut points are 196, 224
and 259.

```r
library(dplyr) # mutate, case_when

births <- births %>% # births = your mfr table, collected, lower-case column names
  mutate(
    ga_weeks = floor(gestationsalder_dage / 7), # completed weeks
    ga_group = case_when(
      is.na(ga_weeks) ~ NA_character_,
      ga_weeks < 28 ~ "extremely preterm",
      ga_weeks < 32 ~ "very preterm",
      ga_weeks < 37 ~ "moderate to late preterm",
      TRUE ~ "term or later"
    )
  )

count(births, ga_group) # missing values show up as their own row
```

### Stillbirth definition changed in 2004 {#stillbirth-2004}

Until 31 March 2004 a stillbirth was a dead fetus delivered after 28 completed
weeks. From 1 April 2004 it is a dead fetus delivered after 22 completed weeks.
Stillbirths between 22 and 28 weeks before April 2004 are in the National
Patient Register but not in the MFR ([Bliddal et al.
2018](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10654-018-0356-1)). A study of stillbirth or
extreme prematurity that crosses 2004 needs to take this into account.

::: {#early-years .callout-note collapse="true" title="Births before 1978, in data from Sundhedsdatastyrelsen (SDS)"}
DST's MFR tables start in 1997, so this only matters if you have older births
from SDS. Before 1978 gestational age was
coded in the variable `fuldb`, with 0 for 40 weeks or more and 1 to 8 for
increasing prematurity. For 1974 to 1977, 89.6% of children were coded 0,
against 70.0% in the later years, so the groups are too coarse to use as
weeks. Gestational age in completed weeks (`svlengde`) is used from 1978 ([á
Rogvi et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0016668)). The same
paper found that SGA in the early years was classified with 49% false
positives, mainly because of these intervals. A cut-off of 3 standard
deviations below the mean brought the false positives down to 9%, at the cost
of more false negatives. The authors note that data from before 1981 are most
often left out. A sensitivity analysis that starts later is a simple way to
check how much the early years matter.
:::

## Small and large for gestational age {#sga-lga}

SGA and LGA compare birth weight with a reference for the same gestational age
and sex. The usual rule is a birth weight below the 10th percentile for SGA and
above the 90th for LGA. Some studies use the 3rd percentile for severe SGA. The
register does not hold a ready-made SGA variable, so you need a reference and
a rule, and you need to report both.

The reference decides who is classified. Three are in common use.

**Marsál (1996).** Curves built from ultrasound estimates of fetal weight in 86
uncomplicated pregnancies at four Scandinavian centres, because curves built
from birth weights underestimate growth in the preterm period. The standard
deviation is set to 12% of the mean weight, and SGA is below the mean minus 2
standard deviations. That is a different rule from the 10th percentile and
classifies a different share of births. Boys weigh 2 to 3% more than girls on
average ([Marsál et al.
1996](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1651-2227.1996.tb14164.x)). The curves were
used to define SGA in the Danish MFR for 1974 to 1996 ([á Rogvi et al.
2011](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0016668)).

**INTERGROWTH-21st.** An international standard for newborn size from healthy
pregnancies in eight populations, with centiles by gestational age and sex
([Villar et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(14)60932-6)). In 15
European countries, SGA and LGA prevalence was near 10% with each country's own
charts. With INTERGROWTH-21st it ranged from 3.0% to 10.1% for SGA and from
8.0% to 24.9% for LGA, along a north to south gradient. Infants who were
reclassified from SGA to normal growth by the international chart still had a
higher perinatal mortality than other normally grown infants (odds ratio 2.7)
([Hocquette et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lanepe.2021.100167)). The
authors conclude that an international chart can classify growth-restricted
infants as normally grown. The paper includes births from 33 weeks.

**Customised references.** These adjust the expected weight for maternal
height, weight, parity and ethnic group ([Gardosi & Francis
1999](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1471-0528.1999.tb08267.x)). They need those
inputs. In the MFR, maternal weight, height and BMI (body mass index) exist from 2003 (see
`bmi_moder`, `hoejde_moder`, `vaegt_moder` in the [column
table](register-reference.qmd#mfr---medical-birth-register)), so a customised
reference is only possible for later births.

For very preterm infants the choice of chart changes the SGA prevalence, and
the chart should be chosen for that age range. Report the chart you used and
repeat the analysis with a second one.

Once you have chosen a chart, copy its cut-off weights into a small table,
`ref`, with one row per sex and completed week, and join it onto the births.
The sketch uses `ga_weeks` from the [preterm code](#preterm) above. In the 2019
table, recode -1 in the birth weight to `NA` first ([Which table holds
what](#tables)).

```r
library(dplyr) # left_join, mutate, case_when, count

# ref: one row per sex and completed week, from the chart you chose
#   koen_barn | ga_weeks | p10 | p90   (p10 and p90 are weights in grams)
# koen_barn must be coded the same way in ref as in births: check with count()
births <- births %>%
  left_join(ref, by = c("koen_barn", "ga_weeks")) %>% # adds p10 and p90 to each birth
  mutate(
    size_for_ga = case_when(
      is.na(vaegt_barn) | is.na(p10) ~ NA_character_, # no weight, or a week the chart does not cover
      vaegt_barn < p10 ~ "SGA",                        # below the 10th percentile
      vaegt_barn > p90 ~ "LGA",                        # above the 90th percentile
      TRUE ~ "AGA"                                     # appropriate for gestational age
    )
  )

count(births, size_for_ga) # missing values show up as their own row
```

### What to report {#report-ga}

- Which gestational age variable you used and what you did with missing and
  implausible values.
- The preterm cut points, and whether you analysed the three groups or one
  composite.
- The growth reference, the rule (percentile or standard deviation) and the
  cut-offs for SGA and LGA.
- Whether the analysis is limited to singletons.
- A sensitivity analysis with a second reference, and one that starts after the
  early years if your study covers them.

## Parity {#parity}

### What the MFR variable means {#parity-definition}

SDS defines `paritet` as the number of completed pregnancies including
stillbirths at the end of the current delivery, so 1 is a first birth
([SDS, documentation
1997-2018](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/Media/638650989745673989/Dokumentation_Foedselsregisteret_1997_2018.xlsx)).
The 2019 documentation uses the same wording, with -1 for not stated. It counts
deliveries, not children, so a twin delivery adds one. The variable is not
gravidity: miscarriages and induced abortions are not part of it.

The midwife records the number of previous live births on the notification form
for the register. A comparison with the parity calculated in DST's fertility
database found that more than 99.5% of women with parity one, who had given
birth from 1978, were classified as such by both ([Knudsen
1993](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8212355/), abstract in English). That is
the evidence for first births only. It does not cover higher parity.

Parity is missing for 1 to 3% of births in the years Bliddal et al. tabulate
([Bliddal et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10654-018-0356-1), Table 5).

From 2019, SDS takes parity from the birth report. If it is missing, or lower
than the number of births the mother has in the MFR, SDS replaces it with the
number of births in the MFR, and the documentation says that only births from
2005 onwards are included in that count ([SDS, documentation from
2019](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/Media/638650989728109987/Dokumentation_Foedselsregisteret_2019_og_frem.xlsx)).
Check the minimum value in your own file before you use the column.

::: {#parity-ftforael .callout-note collapse="true" title="Parity in DST's fertility data (`ftforael`, `ftbarn`)"}
DST's fertility datasets hold their own parity columns. `medicinsk_paritet` in
`ftforael` is the child's birth number for the mother. Stillbirths count and a
multiple birth counts as one. DST adds that children not known in the registers
are not counted, such as children born abroad who never received a CPR number,
and children born before 1960 ([DST,
MEDICINSK_PARITET](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/Times/fertilitetsdatabasen/medicinsk-paritet)).
DST gives no definition of the other parity columns beyond a short label, see
[the column table](register-reference.qmd#ftbarn). `paritet` in `ftforael` is
"the mother's delivery number as stated in the MFR" ([DST,
PARITET](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/Times/fertilitetsdatabasen/paritet)).

If you count parity from `ftbarn`, keep presumed biological mothers first:
codes 21 to 23 of `mor_foed_adop` ([DST,
MOR_FOED_ADOP](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/Times/fertilitetsdatabasen/mor-foed-adop)).
What the codes mean, and what they cannot tell you, is under
[Adoption](family-links.qmd#adoption) in Family links.
:::

### Deriving parity from successive births {#parity-derive}

You can count the mother's earlier deliveries yourself, to check `paritet` or
when it is missing. The MFR has one row per child, so a twin delivery gives two
rows. The code below treats births to the same mother at most one day apart as
one delivery, the rule DST uses for `flerfold` ([Multiple
births](#multiples-records)), so twins born either side of midnight stay
together. It also gives each delivery an id, `delivery_id`, which the
[multiple-births code](#multiples-approaches) uses.

In the 2019 table `DW_EK_Foedsel` is the key of the birth event, shared by the
children of one delivery ([the Nyfoedte
section](register-reference.qmd#mfr-nyfoedte)). In the 1997-2018 table SDS
describes `foedselsloebenummer` only as the birth serial number, so check with
`count()` whether twins share a value before you rely on it.

```r
library(dplyr) # count, filter, arrange, group_by, mutate, ungroup, select

# births = your mfr table, collected, lower-case column names, one row per child

# A row without the mother's number or the birth date cannot be placed in a
# delivery. Count them, so you can report how many you leave out
count(births, no_mother_or_date = is.na(cpr_moder) | is.na(foedselsdato))

births <- births %>%
  filter(!is.na(cpr_moder), !is.na(foedselsdato)) %>% # one NA would make every later count NA
  arrange(cpr_moder, foedselsdato) %>%                 # each mother's children in date order
  group_by(cpr_moder) %>%
  mutate(
    # TRUE for the first child of a delivery: the mother's first child in the
    # table, or a child born more than one day after her previous child
    new_delivery   = c(TRUE, diff(foedselsdato) > 1),
    # running count of her deliveries: 1 = her first delivery in the table
    parity_derived = cumsum(new_delivery)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # one id per delivery, shared by twins: the mother plus her delivery number
  mutate(delivery_id = paste(cpr_moder, parity_derived))

# one row per delivery (its first child), for the time-varying code below
deliveries <- births %>%
  filter(new_delivery) %>%
  select(cpr_moder, foedselsdato, parity_derived)
```

The count only sees deliveries that are in your table. A table that starts in
1997 undercounts parity for women who gave birth earlier. Compare the derived
value with `paritet`: derived values below the recorded ones are expected for
women with earlier births outside your table.

### Parity that changes during follow-up {#parity-time-varying}

If you follow women across several pregnancies, parity changes at each
delivery, and a baseline value is wrong after the next one. Build start/stop
rows with `tmerge()` as in [Time-varying variables](time-varying.qmd#a-time-varying-covariate),
with each delivery as a measurement. The table you hand to `tmerge()` needs
the delivery day on the same scale as follow-up, and the parity after the
delivery.

```r
library(dplyr) # left_join, mutate, transmute

# index_dates: cpr_moder, index_date (start of follow-up for each woman)
measurements <- deliveries %>%
  left_join(index_dates, by = "cpr_moder") %>%
  transmute(
    pnr = cpr_moder,
    day = as.numeric(foedselsdato - index_date),
    value = parity_derived
  )
# a negative day sets the value at the start of follow-up; see the time-varying page
```

### Women who gave birth abroad {#parity-immigrants}

The MFR does not include births that took place abroad ([Bliddal et al.
2018](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10654-018-0356-1)). A woman who immigrated
after earlier births has a first MFR birth that looks like a first birth when
you derive parity from the table. In the Norwegian register, migrant women
whose first birth was before arrival had higher odds of preterm birth,
stillbirth and low Apgar score in later births than migrant women whose first
birth was in Norway, so the group is not a random subset ([Vik et al.
2020](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-020-05415-y)). The sources on this page do
not say whether the recorded `paritet` counts births abroad, so do not assume
that it does.

Options, depending on your question:

- Stratify or restrict by origin, for example women born in Denmark. `ie_type`
  and `opr_land` in BEF (the population register) give immigrant status and country of origin, see
  [Immigrants and descendants](immigrants-and-descendants.qmd).
- Run the analysis without immigrant women as a sensitivity analysis.
- State the limitation in the methods and give the share of immigrant women in
  the study population.

### What to report {#report-parity}

- Whether parity is the recorded `paritet` or derived, and which table and
  years it was derived from.
- Whether it is fixed at baseline or time-varying.
- How women with earlier births abroad were handled, and how many there are.

## Multiple births {#multiples}

### How they appear in the MFR {#multiples-records}

A multiple birth is a delivery of more than one child. The register unit is
the child, live-born or stillborn ([SDS, register declaration,
section 1.2](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/Media/638650989716795161/Registerdeklaration%20for%20foedselsregisteret.pdf)),
so a twin delivery gives two rows. Bliddal et al. count 1,249 multiple
deliveries among 66,917 in 1997 and 1,064 among 61,687 in 2016, about 2% in
each of the years they list ([Bliddal et al.
2018](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10654-018-0356-1), Table 3). The table has more
infants than deliveries for the same reason.

You can identify them in three ways. Use the column names as your delivery spells them.

| Source | Column | Note |
| ------ | ------ | ---- |
| Number of children | `AntalBoernIFoedslen` (2019 onwards) | Number of children in the birth: 1, 2, 3 ([SDS, documentation from 2019](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/Media/638650989728109987/Dokumentation_Foedselsregisteret_2019_og_frem.xlsx)). For 1997-2018, count the rows per mother and birth date. |
| Child's order | `flerfoldsfoedsel_beregnet`, `barnsnummer_flerfoldsfoedsel` (1997-2018), `BarnsNummerIFoedslen` (2019 onwards) | The child's number within the birth ([SDS, documentation 1997-2018](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/Media/638650989745673989/Dokumentation_Foedselsregisteret_1997_2018.xlsx)). |
| Diagnosis | `flerfoldsgraviditet` | An ICD-10 code. O30 is multiple gestation: O30.0 twin, O30.1 triplet, O30.2 quadruplet, O30.8 other, O30.9 unspecified ([WHO ICD-10](https://icd.who.int/browse10/2019/en#/O30)). Check how the code is written in your delivery with `count()`. |

Use two of them and check that they agree. In the fertility data, `flerfold` in
`ftbarn` is 1 single, 2 twin, 3 triplet and 4 quadruplet. DST derives it from
the MFR and CPR. Children are grouped as a multiple birth if they have the same
mother and birth dates at most one day apart, and for births registered in the
MFR if their birth dates are less than 30 days apart ([DST,
FLERFOLD](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/Times/fertilitetsdatabasen/flerfold)).

### Multiple birth as mediator, confounder or collider {#multiples-causal}

What to do with multiple births depends on the question, so draw the causal
diagram first. In a study of assisted reproduction and preterm birth,
plurality lies on the path from exposure to outcome, and adjusting for it
blocks part of the effect. In a study of maternal age, plurality can be a
confounder. When plurality and the outcome share a cause that is not
measured, conditioning on it can open a path that was closed, which is
collider bias. These are examples, not a rule for your study.

Restricting to singletons, analysing at the pregnancy level and analysing at
the infant level answer different questions and give different estimands
([Brown et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000001809)). Choose the
one that matches the question and say why.

### Approaches {#multiples-approaches}

- **Restrict to singletons.** Common for birth weight, fetal growth and
  preterm birth, where the process differs in multiples. It conditions on
  plurality, so it changes the question if plurality is on the causal path.
- **Pregnancy level.** One row per delivery, with the outcome set to 1 if any
  child had it. Fits questions about the pregnancy.
- **Infant level with clustering.** All children, with the dependence between
  children of the same delivery taken into account.

For a binary outcome at the infant level, a simulation study with preterm
infants found that generalised estimating equations (GEE) gave the best
balance between standard error and parameter estimate at any share of twins. A
logistic random-intercept model could not estimate the correlation between
siblings when twins were few, and gave results like ordinary logistic
regression. Ordinary logistic regression underestimated all parameters when
twins were present ([Sauzet & Peacock
2017](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12874-017-0369-6)).

The sketch needs `delivery_id`, which the [parity code](#parity-derive) above
gives each delivery. In the 2019 table `dw_ek_foedsel` can be used instead.

```r
library(dplyr)   # mutate, arrange
library(geepack) # geeglm()

# births: one row per child, with delivery_id from the parity code above
births <- births %>%
  mutate(delivery_id = factor(delivery_id)) %>% # a character id is read as ONE cluster, without an error
  arrange(delivery_id)                          # geeglm wants the rows of a cluster next to each other

fit <- geeglm(preterm ~ exposure + parity_cat,  # preterm 0/1, your exposure and covariates
              id = delivery_id,                 # children of the same delivery form a cluster
              family = binomial,
              corstr = "exchangeable",          # the same correlation between any two children of a delivery
              data = births)
summary(fit)
```

If twins are the subject of the study, the Danish Twin Registry holds twins
from birth cohorts to 2009, linked to the national registers at Statistics
Denmark ([Pedersen et al. 2019](https://doi.org/10.1017/thg.2019.72)). A review
of 32 twin studies of early-life exposures describes conditional (within-pair)
methods, which adjust by design for shared confounders, and marginal methods
such as GEE, which treat pairs as clusters and which the authors say may give
invalid inference for within-pair questions ([Fasola et al.
2021](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182312696)).

### Multiples and parity together {#multiples-parity}

A twin delivery adds one to parity, not two. When you count deliveries from
the MFR, group the children of one delivery before you count, as in [the
derivation above](#parity-derive).

### What to report {#report-multiples}

- The approach (singletons only, pregnancy level or infant level) and why.
- The variable or code used to identify multiple births.
- The method used to account for clustering, if you kept all children.
- The share of multiple births in the study population.
